IN PHOTOS: A dense layer of toxic smog blankets the capital’s skyline as a continuing fire at the Navotas sanitary landfill worsens air quality across Metro Manila. Captured on April 27, 2026, the aerial scene shows heavy particulate haze drifting over residential areas and major roads, reducing visibility and heightening health concerns for millions of residents.

Meanwhile, the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) has ordered all sanitary landfill operators to submit contingency plans for emergency response, nearly two weeks after the blaze at the Navotas site began.

📸: Edd Castro

The Japanese government is preparing to revise the Self-Defense Forces (SDF) Act to permit, under “special exceptions,” transfer of surplus defense equipment—including lethal weapons—to foreign governments either free or below market price, the Yomiuri Shimbun reported Sunday. The amendment is targeted for the Diet’s regular session next year, with the necessity stated explicitly in the revised National Security Strategy this year.

Global Times reports that the SDF Act revision is the mechanism for revising the April 21 revision of Japan’s Three Principles on Transfer of Defense Equipment and Technology, which lifted the prohibition on exporting weapons with lethal capabilities. Concrete deals are already in negotiation. The Philippines is considering acquiring the “Abukuma"-class destroyer escort—which would be the first Japanese export of a used destroyer escort. Indonesia has expressed interest in the “Oyashio"-class submarine. Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi is scheduled to visit both countries in May.

The export pivot is part of an accelerating Japanese military repositioning. Japan is currently participating, with 1,400 personnel, in the U.S.-Philippines Balikatan 2026 joint exercise (April 20-May 8), featuring live-fire operations in northern Luzon facing the Taiwan Strait.

Japanese press response has been sharp. The Tokyo Shimbun editorialized April 22 that the policy reversal amounts to “shallow thinking that damages pacifism” and that the ruling LDP-Ishin coalition rammed through the change in just three sessions—versus 27 sessions of consultation when the rules were last revised in 2024. The Tokyo Shimbun also recalled a 1976 Diet statement by then-Foreign Minister Kiichi Miyazawa: “Japan has not fallen so low as to make money by exporting weapons.” Asked about that line in Diet testimony in March 2026, Takaichi dismissed it: “The times have changed.” A Kyodo poll the same month found 56% of the Japanese public opposed to lethal weapons exports, against approximately 36% in favor—a 20-point margin that the Cabinet ignored.

Article 9 has been incrementally drained of content over the past decade: collective self-defense, long-range strike capability, now lethal arms exports. The country that committed the attack on Pearl Harbor and the Rape of Nanking is being rearmed for what the Anglosphere calls the Indo-Pacific.
